data.content_ref: inline:SRC_004 proposes the 'Latent Trigger' test: check whether failure correlation spikes when an environmental variable changes, versus staying constant under true independence. But this is only sufficient under one evidentiary regime — discrete, observable environmental shifts. The problem asks to distinguish failures that are truly independent from failures that merely appear uncorrelated until a shared cause is found. SRC_04's own counterconditions concede the gap: a slow-burn shared degradation (e.g., a monotonic clock drift, gradual certificate expiry, creeping disk wear, slowly corrupting shared dataset) need not align with any discrete event, so its temporal-clustering test would report constant low correlation and falsely classify the failure as independent. The test therefore lacks the covering principle needed for the general case; it detects a subset of latent triggers (event-aligned) while remaining silent on the rest. Without a complementary mechanism (e.g., counterfactual/shared-dependency graph analysis, prospective stress tests of hypothesized common causes) it does not provide the evidence the problem demands.
